claim: Duan et al. propose a position-based, force-feedback variable-impedance filter for tracking contact force when environment stiffness is unknown and the contact location changes along a surface. The method does not estimate or optimize a full impedance matrix: it sets the virtual stiffness to zero, keeps virtual mass fixed, and adapts an additive virtual-damping term through an accumulated sampled force error. The paper derives a scalar stability bound, 0<sigma<lambda b/(m+lambda b), after approximating the delayed error dynamics, and establishes zero steady force error for a stable step-input case. Simulations and ESTUN ER16 experiments report recovery on slope and curved surfaces, but the displayed analysis is not a full nonlinear robot/contact stability proof and does not prove exact tracking for arbitrary dynamic desired forces.
claim_locator: Abstract, p. 54: Defines the uncertain environment as unknown geometrical and mechanical properties, describes position-based impedance control using measured contact-force feedback, and claims online impedance adjustment for dynamic desired-force tracking.

Section 2.2, equations (1)-(5), pp. 56-57: Derives the conventional linear position-based impedance filter and shows that zero steady force error ordinarily requires knowledge of environment location x_e and stiffness k_e.

Section 3.1, equations (6)-(10), p. 57: Replaces the reference position with the initial environment location and sets virtual stiffness k=0 so that unknown environment stiffness does not enter the steady-state error through a nonzero virtual spring term.

Section 3.2, equations (11)-(15), p. 57: Keeps mass m fixed, varies damping as b+Delta b(t), and defines Delta b(t)=(b/dot(hat e)(t))Phi(t), with Phi updated from the previous sampled force error at rate sigma.

Section 4, equations (16)-(30), pp. 57-58: Reduces the scalar delayed force-error dynamics to a characteristic equation, invokes a sufficiently long accumulated-error series and the approximation exp(-lambda s) approximately 1-lambda s, then applies the Routh criterion to obtain 0<sigma<lambda b/(m+lambda b).

Section 4, equations (31)-(34), p. 58: Uses a final-value calculation for a step input r(s)=1/s to conclude c(t)=f_d(t)-f_e(t) tends to zero for the stable approximated system; exact convergence for sinusoidal input is asserted afterward but not separately derived.

Section 5.1, equations (35) and Figures 5-19, pp. 59-62: Reports disturbance-free Simulink comparisons on planar, sloped, sinusoidal, and complex surfaces, including stiffness jumps and a time-varying desired force.

Section 5.2, Figures 20-26, pp. 62-64: Reports ESTUN ER16 experiments with a wrist force sensor and 5 ms communications on flat, slope, and blended rigid-curved/plastic-flat surfaces separated by a groove.
epistemic_status: approximation-based analytical stability condition with author-reported simulation and hardware evidence
problem_and_setting: The paper studies one-dimensional normal contact-force tracking implemented around a position-controlled industrial robot. The robot/end-effector and environment are represented by linear mass-spring-damper relations after contact, with the environment further simplified to a linear spring of unknown stiffness k_e at a location x_e that may vary along a slope or curved surface. A wrist force sensor measures f_e, and a position-based impedance, operationally an admittance-like force-error-to-commanded-position filter, modifies the reference sent to the robot servo. The targeted uncertainties are unknown or changing environment stiffness and geometrical variation of the contact location; the brief, strongly nonlinear collision phase is acknowledged but not modeled by the stability analysis.
method_or_mechanism: For unknown stiffness, the method removes the virtual spring term by setting k=0, yielding m ddot(e)+b dot(e)+k_e e=-f_d after contact; m and b remain design parameters, with the text saying they are chosen using an approximation of k_e. For a time-varying environment location, the paper introduces an estimated location hat(x_e) and error hat(e), holds m fixed, and makes the damping coefficient b+Delta b(t). The adaptive term is Delta b(t)=b Phi(t)/dot(hat(e))(t), while Phi(t)=Phi(t-lambda)+sigma[f_d(t-lambda)-f_e(t-lambda)]/b. Consequently, Delta b dot(hat(e)) equals an accumulated force-error compensation term. The resulting commanded acceleration, velocity, and position are integrated discretely and passed through inverse kinematics and the position servo. Thus, the variable impedance is specifically a scalar damping adjustment combined with zero virtual stiffness; it is not adaptation of robot dynamics, a learned state-dependent stiffness matrix, or cost-optimal impedance selection.
content_summary: The paper first shows that conventional constant position-based impedance force tracking has a steady error unless environment location and stiffness are known. It then separates the uncertainty problem into stiffness and location. Setting virtual stiffness to zero removes one source of steady-state bias for unknown k_e, while a sampled integral-like force-error state changes virtual damping to compensate dynamic location error. A transfer-function analysis of the delayed scalar contact dynamics produces a Routh stability condition after a first-order delay approximation. The final-value calculation directly covers a step input and yields zero steady force error c=f_d-f_e if the approximated system is stable. Simulations compare fixed and adaptive impedance on flat, slope, sine, and complex surfaces; fixed impedance handles planar stiffness jumps but retains bias or fails to converge on moving surfaces, while the adaptive method is reported to track both constant and time-varying force commands. Hardware tests use an ESTUN ER16 robot, Optoforce wrist sensor, 5 ms EtherCAT/UDP cycles, and a pulley end effector. Fixed impedance is tested on a flat surface, and adaptive impedance on slope and blended curved/grooved surfaces. The reported force settles near -12 N in about 15 s on the flat and slope trials; on the composite surface, the trace contains error and a large transient around the groove/stiffness change, followed by recovery by roughly 31 s.
synthesis_role: This paper represents a pragmatic branch of VIC development focused on force regulation for position-controlled industrial robots: instead of learning a general impedance policy or identifying a complete environment model, it analytically removes virtual stiffness and adapts damping from measured force error. It demonstrates that narrowly structured impedance adaptation can compensate geometry-induced force bias online, while also exposing the gap between a task-specific scalar convergence analysis and general stability guarantees for variable impedance under contact transitions.
development_link: Relative to early direct adaptive impedance control, this method does not adapt manipulator dynamic parameters or directly shape a torque-level closed-loop impedance; it operates as an outer position-command filter and changes only a scalar damping compensation term after setting virtual stiffness to zero. Relative to optimal impedance adaptation, it defines no interaction cost, critical-point condition, or optimization over impedance parameters; sigma is an update gain constrained by an approximate stability calculation. Its contribution is therefore not a more general adaptive-control theorem but a simpler force-error-driven mechanism for uncertain surface following, with later VIC work still needing full-robot stability, multidimensional impedance representations, contact-transition treatment, and robust implementation near singular adaptive-law denominators.

evidence.statement: Equations (2)-(5) derive the constant-impedance steady error and show that exact cancellation ordinarily requires x_r=x_e-f_d/k_e, which depends on unknown environment location and stiffness.
Equations (9)-(14) set virtual stiffness k to zero, retain mass m, and adapt damping through Delta b=b Phi/dot(hat e), where Phi accumulates sampled desired-minus-measured force error.

Equations (24)-(30) approximate the delayed characteristic equation using an infinite accumulated-error series and exp(-lambda s) approximately 1-lambda s, then use a Routh array to obtain 0<sigma<lambda b/(m+lambda b).
Equations (31)-(34) use the final-value theorem with step input r(s)=1/s to conclude c(t)=f_d-f_e tends to zero for the stable approximated scalar dynamics.

With k=0 and m=1, fixed impedance tracked 5 N on a plane despite k_e jumps from 1000 to 3000 to 5000 N/m; on a slope with k_e=5000 N/m and f_d=50 N, fixed impedance settled near 65 N whereas adaptive impedance with initial b=100 and sigma=0.5 reached the desired value after adjustment.

On sinusoidal and complex surfaces, the paper reports nonconvergence or bias for fixed impedance and near-zero force error for the adaptive method; a complex-surface simulation also tracks a time-varying desired force. The simulation explicitly excludes disturbances.

An ESTUN ER16 with an Optoforce HEX-70-XE-1000N wrist sensor and 5 ms communication cycles followed 40 cm surface paths at f_d=-12 N. Flat fixed-impedance and slope adaptive trials settled in about 15 s; the composite-surface adaptive trial traversed a groove, experienced a stiffness change at about 28 s, and recovered by about 31 s.

boundary_conditions: The analytical result is one-dimensional and applies after contact to a linear spring environment and second-order virtual impedance; it does not cover the strongly nonlinear collision interval that the paper explicitly identifies.
Only the virtual damping is adapted. Virtual stiffness is fixed at zero and virtual mass is fixed; the method does not learn a full stiffness/damping matrix or an arbitrary state-dependent impedance.

The controller still uses an estimated environment location and its derivatives through hat(e); adaptation compensates residual location error rather than eliminating all environment-state estimation requirements.
The text says m and b are selected using an approximation of environment stiffness even though exact k_e is not required, so performance is not parameter-free.

The stability bound follows from a sufficiently long accumulated-error series, a sufficiently fast sampling assumption, and the first-order approximation exp(-lambda s) approximately 1-lambda s; it is not a necessary-and-sufficient result for the original delayed system.

The displayed convergence calculation directly treats a step r(s), not a general time-varying desired force. Sinusoidal and series-valued desired-force tracking is supported by assertion and simulation, not by the shown final-value derivation.

No Lyapunov, passivity, input-to-state stability, or robustness proof is provided for the complete nonlinear robot, servo, inverse kinematics, sensor, sampled-data implementation, or environment interaction.
Simulation evidence uses the same simplified contact model and explicitly excludes disturbances.

The hardware study does not compare fixed and adaptive control on identical surfaces: fixed impedance is used for the flat trial, while adaptive control is used for slope and composite-surface trials.
Hardware dynamic desired-force tracking is not demonstrated; the robot experiments use a constant -12 N command, while time-varying desired force appears in simulation.
assumptions: After contact, measured robot position tracks commanded position closely enough to take X_c=X_m.
The relevant Cartesian directions are decoupled so that a one-dimensional normal-force analysis represents the controlled interaction.
Environment contact is a positive linear stiffness relation f_e=k_e(x_e-x_c), even when k_e changes between regions.
The force sensor, inverse kinematics, position servo, and numerical integrations operate with negligible dynamics beyond those included in the scalar model.
The environment-location estimate and its velocity/acceleration terms are available for the commanded-position recursion.
The adaptive denominator dot(hat e) is nonzero or otherwise handled, although the paper does not specify a regularization or projection rule.
Sampling is sufficiently fast for the first-order delay approximation, and sigma satisfies the derived bound throughout operation.
The closed-loop poles of the approximated characteristic equation are stable so that the final-value theorem is applicable.

reported: Changing the virtual mass online is discouraged because the authors state that it can make the system oscillate.
Fixed impedance tracks planar force through stiffness changes in the reported simulation but settles with substantial bias on a slope and fails to converge on a sinusoidal surface.
The composite-surface hardware experiment retains some force error and shows a pronounced transient while crossing the groove and stiffness transition before recovering.
The paper acknowledges that contact collision is transient and strongly nonlinear, but its proposed post-contact analysis does not model that phase.
The simulations do not include disturbances.
inferred: Because Delta b divides by dot(hat e), the adaptive law is singular or noise-sensitive when estimated relative velocity approaches zero; no saturation, projection, positivity, or regularization mechanism is specified.

The Routh bound certifies only the Taylor-approximated scalar delay model. Stability of the original sampled nonlinear robot-contact loop, especially under actuator limits and communication delay, remains unestablished.

The step-input final-value derivation does not justify the broad statement that tracking error always converges to zero for sinusoidal or arbitrary dynamic desired force; those cases remain simulation-supported only.
Setting virtual stiffness to zero solves a steady-force-bias mechanism but prevents simultaneous prescription of a nonzero target stiffness, limiting general variable-impedance behavior.

Because hardware baselines are not tested on matched uncertain surfaces and no repeated-trial statistics are reported, the experiments establish feasibility but not a controlled quantitative superiority claim.
